questions.question: Let $\underset{\sim}{a}=\begin{pmatrix}3\\-2\end{pmatrix}$. What is the value of $|\underset{\sim}{a}|$?
If $f(x)=\sin^{-1}(x-1)$, which of the following is the range of $f(x)$?
questions.answer: The inverse sine function takes principal values only, so its range is $\left[-\dfrac\pi2,\dfrac\pi2\right]$. The substitution $x\mapsto x-1$ shifts the domain (to $[0,2]$) but does not change the range (B).

questions.question: Which of the following vectors is perpendicular to $\begin{pmatrix}2\\3\end{pmatrix}$?
questions.answer: Perpendicular vectors have zero dot product: $\begin{pmatrix}2\\3\end{pmatrix}\cdot\begin{pmatrix}3\\-2\end{pmatrix}=6-6=0$ (C).

questions.question: A headmaster realises that there is at least one month of the year when at least 34 pupils have a birthday. What is the minimum possible number of pupils at the school?
questions.answer: If every month had at most 33 birthdays there would be at most $12\times33=396$ pupils. So with 397 pupils (pigeonhole principle) at least one month has at least 34. The minimum is 397 (B).

questions.question: A particle moves so that $x=\tan t$ and $y=x^2$. Which of the following is equal to $\dfrac{dy}{dt}$?
questions.answer: $y=\tan^2t$, so $\dfrac{dy}{dt}=2\tan t\sec^2t$ (C).

questions.question: Let $\underset{\sim}{a}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\end{pmatrix}$ and $\underset{\sim}{b}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}$. The projection of $\underset{\sim}{a}$ onto $\underset{\sim}{b}$ is $\lambda\underset{\sim}{b}$. What is the value of $\lambda$?
questions.answer: $\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf b}\mathbf a=\dfrac{\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b}{|\mathbf b|^2}\mathbf b$, so $\lambda=\dfrac{2+2}{1+4}=\dfrac45$ (C).

questions.question: The graphs of $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$ are shown. Which transformation maps $f(x)$ to $g(x)$?
questions.answer: $g$ is symmetric in the $y$-axis, so the right-hand part of $f$ is reflected in the $y$-axis ($f(|x|)$). The result has parts below the $x$-axis, and $g$ has none, so these are reflected above the axis too: $g(x)=|f(|x|)|$ (D).

questions.question: Which of the following slope fields corresponds to the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{y-x}x$? (Slope fields A, B, C, D are shown in order.)
questions.answer: $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac yx-1$. Horizontal line elements occur along $y=x$. The equation is undefined at $x=0$, so there are no line elements on the $y$-axis. Along $y=0$, $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-1$. The gradient changes sign on either side of $y=x$. Only slope field D has all these features (D).

questions.question: The nine members of the Fellowship of the Ring are seated randomly around a circular table. What is the probability that the two youngest members of the Fellowship are seated next to each other?
questions.answer: Total circular arrangements of 9 people: $8!$. Treat the two youngest as one block: 8 objects in a circle give $7!$ arrangements, and the block can be ordered internally in $2!$ ways. Probability $=\dfrac{7!\,2!}{8!}$ (D).

questions.question: Let $g(x)=\sin^2x-\dfrac x3$. How many times does the graph of $y=g(x)$ intersect the $x$-axis?
questions.answer: Solve $\sin^2x=\dfrac x3$. Since $0\le\sin^2x\le1$, solutions satisfy $0\le x\le3$. $x=0$ is a solution. $g(1)=\sin^21-\dfrac13>0$ while $g\left(\dfrac14\right)=\sin^2\dfrac14-\dfrac1{12}<0$, so there is a root in $\left(\dfrac14,1\right)$. $g\left(\dfrac\pi2\right)=1-\dfrac\pi6>0$ and $g(\pi)=-\dfrac\pi3<0$, so there is a root in $\left(\dfrac\pi2,\pi\right)$. Graphically, $y=\sin^2x$ meets the line $y=\dfrac x3$ three times in all (C).

questions.question: How many four-digit numbers can be formed using the digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 without repetition?
questions.answer: ${}^7P_4=7\times6\times5\times4=840$.

questions.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^1\dfrac2{1+x^2}dx$.
questions.answer: $2\Big[\tan^{-1}x\Big]_0^1=2\left(\dfrac\pi4-0\right)=\dfrac\pi2$.

questions.question: Use the substitution $t=\tan\dfrac\theta2$ to solve $2\sin\theta+\cos\theta=2$, for $0\le\theta\le2\pi$.
questions.answer: $\sin\theta=\dfrac{2t}{1+t^2}$ and $\cos\theta=\dfrac{1-t^2}{1+t^2}$. $\dfrac{4t+1-t^2}{1+t^2}=2$, so $1+4t-t^2=2+2t^2$, i.e. $3t^2-4t+1=0$ and $(3t-1)(t-1)=0$. $t=\dfrac13$ or $t=1$. $\dfrac\theta2=\tan^{-1}\dfrac13$ or $\dfrac\pi4$, so $\theta=2\tan^{-1}\dfrac13\ (\approx0.644)$ or $\theta=\dfrac\pi2$. (Check: $\theta=\pi$, where $t$ is undefined, gives $-1\ne2$, so it is not a solution.)

questions.question: The curve $C$ is defined parametrically by $x=t^2+1$ and $y=t^3-3t$. Find the gradient of the tangent to $C$ when $t=2$.
questions.answer: $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=2t$ and $\dfrac{dy}{dt}=3t^2-3$, so $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{3t^2-3}{2t}$. At $t=2$: $\dfrac{12-3}4=\dfrac94$.

questions.question: The area, $A$, of a square is increasing at a rate of $12\ \text{cm}^2\text{s}^{-1}$. Find the rate at which the side length, $x$, is increasing when the side length is 3 cm.
questions.answer: $A=x^2$, so $\dfrac{dA}{dt}=2x\dfrac{dx}{dt}$. $12=2(3)\dfrac{dx}{dt}$, so $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=2$ cm/s.

questions.question: Express $\cos2x+\sin2x$ in the form $R\cos(2x-\alpha)$, where $R>0$ and $0<\alpha<\dfrac\pi2$.
questions.answer: $R\cos(2x-\alpha)=R\cos\alpha\cos2x+R\sin\alpha\sin2x$, so $R\cos\alpha=1$ and $R\sin\alpha=1$. $R=\sqrt2$ and $\tan\alpha=1$, so $\alpha=\dfrac\pi4$. $\cos2x+\sin2x=\sqrt2\cos\left(2x-\dfrac\pi4\right)$.

questions.question: Hence solve $\cos2x+\sin2x=1$ for $0\le x\le2\pi$.
questions.answer: $\sqrt2\cos\left(2x-\dfrac\pi4\right)=1$, so $\cos\left(2x-\dfrac\pi4\right)=\dfrac1{\sqrt2}$ with $-\dfrac\pi4\le2x-\dfrac\pi4\le\dfrac{15\pi}4$. So $2x-\dfrac\pi4=-\dfrac\pi4,\dfrac\pi4,\dfrac{7\pi}4,\dfrac{9\pi}4,\dfrac{15\pi}4$, giving $2x=0,\dfrac\pi2,2\pi,\dfrac{5\pi}2,4\pi$ and $x=0,\dfrac\pi4,\pi,\dfrac{5\pi}4,2\pi$.

questions.question: Let $u=\sqrt x$. Hence evaluate $\displaystyle\int_1^4\dfrac1{\sqrt x\left(1+\sqrt x\right)}dx$.
questions.answer: $x=u^2$, $dx=2u\,du$; $x=1\to u=1$ and $x=4\to u=2$. $\displaystyle\int_1^2\dfrac{2u}{u(1+u)}du=2\int_1^2\dfrac1{1+u}du=2\Big[\ln(1+u)\Big]_1^2=2(\ln3-\ln2)=2\ln\dfrac32\ \left(=\ln\dfrac94\right)$.

questions.question: Solve $\dfrac x{x+1}>3$.
questions.answer: Multiply by $(x+1)^2>0$ ($x\ne-1$): $x(x+1)>3(x+1)^2$, so $0>3(x+1)^2-x(x+1)=(x+1)(2x+3)$. This holds between the roots: $-\dfrac32<x<-1$.

questions.question: Let $\underset{\sim}{a}=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\5\end{pmatrix}$ and $\underset{\sim}{b}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}$. Find the angle between $\underset{\sim}{a}$ and $\underset{\sim}{b}$. Give your answer in exact form.
questions.answer: $\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b=-2+10=8$, $|\mathbf a|=\sqrt{29}$, $|\mathbf b|=\sqrt5$. $\cos\theta=\dfrac8{\sqrt{145}}$, so $\theta=\cos^{-1}\dfrac8{\sqrt{145}}$.

questions.question: Let $\underset{\sim}{a}=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\5\end{pmatrix}$ and $\underset{\sim}{b}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}$. Find $\lambda$, given that $\underset{\sim}{c}=\underset{\sim}{b}+\lambda\underset{\sim}{a}$ is perpendicular to $\underset{\sim}{a}$.
questions.answer: $\mathbf c\cdot\mathbf a=\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf a+\lambda|\mathbf a|^2=8+29\lambda=0$, so $\lambda=-\dfrac8{29}$.

questions.question: Let $\underset{\sim}{a}=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\5\end{pmatrix}$ and $\underset{\sim}{b}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}$. Find the area of the parallelogram with adjacent sides $\underset{\sim}{a}$ and $\underset{\sim}{b}$.
questions.answer: Area $=|\mathbf a||\mathbf b|\sin\theta$ with $\cos\theta=\dfrac8{\sqrt{145}}$, so $\sin\theta=\dfrac9{\sqrt{145}}$ and area $=\sqrt{145}\cdot\dfrac9{\sqrt{145}}=9$ square units. (Alternatively, $|(-2)(2)-(5)(1)|=9$.)

questions.question: Prove that $\tan\theta=\dfrac{\sin2\theta}{1+\cos2\theta}$.
questions.answer: $\dfrac{\sin2\theta}{1+\cos2\theta}=\dfrac{2\sin\theta\cos\theta}{1+2\cos^2\theta-1}=\dfrac{2\sin\theta\cos\theta}{2\cos^2\theta}=\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}=\tan\theta$.

questions.question: Use mathematical induction to prove that $7^n-1$ is divisible by 6 for all positive integers $n$.
questions.answer:
$n=1$: $7-1=6=6\times1$, true.

Assume $7^k-1=6M$ for some integer $M$. Then $7^{k+1}-1=7\cdot7^k-1=7(6M+1)-1=42M+6=6(7M+1)$, which is divisible by 6 since $7M+1$ is an integer. So true for $n=k+1$. By induction, true for all positive integers $n$.

questions.question: Let $O$, $A$ and $B$ be three points. Let $\underset{\sim}{a}=\overrightarrow{OA}$ and $\underset{\sim}{b}=\overrightarrow{OB}$. Points $P$ and $Q$ lie on $AB$ such that $AP:PB=1:2$ and $AQ:QB=2:1$. Express $\overrightarrow{OP}$ and $\overrightarrow{OQ}$ in terms of $\underset{\sim}{a}$ and $\underset{\sim}{b}$.
questions.answer: $\overrightarrow{AB}=\mathbf b-\mathbf a$. $\overrightarrow{OP}=\mathbf a+\dfrac13(\mathbf b-\mathbf a)=\dfrac23\mathbf a+\dfrac13\mathbf b$. $\overrightarrow{OQ}=\mathbf a+\dfrac23(\mathbf b-\mathbf a)=\dfrac13\mathbf a+\dfrac23\mathbf b$.

questions.question: Let $O$, $A$ and $B$ be three points. Let $\underset{\sim}{a}=\overrightarrow{OA}$ and $\underset{\sim}{b}=\overrightarrow{OB}$. Points $P$ and $Q$ lie on $AB$ such that $AP:PB=1:2$ and $AQ:QB=2:1$. Show that $\overrightarrow{PQ}=\dfrac13(\underset{\sim}{b}-\underset{\sim}{a})$.
questions.answer: $\overrightarrow{PQ}=\overrightarrow{OQ}-\overrightarrow{OP}=\left(\dfrac13\mathbf a+\dfrac23\mathbf b\right)-\left(\dfrac23\mathbf a+\dfrac13\mathbf b\right)=\dfrac13(\mathbf b-\mathbf a)$.

questions.question: Let $O$, $A$ and $B$ be three points. Let $\underset{\sim}{a}=\overrightarrow{OA}$ and $\underset{\sim}{b}=\overrightarrow{OB}$. Points $P$ and $Q$ lie on $AB$ such that $AP:PB=1:2$ and $AQ:QB=2:1$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $AB$. Use vectors to show that $\overrightarrow{PM}=\overrightarrow{MQ}$.
questions.answer: $\overrightarrow{OM}=\dfrac12(\mathbf a+\mathbf b)$. $\overrightarrow{PM}=\overrightarrow{OM}-\overrightarrow{OP}=\dfrac12(\mathbf a+\mathbf b)-\dfrac23\mathbf a-\dfrac13\mathbf b=\dfrac16(\mathbf b-\mathbf a)$. $\overrightarrow{MQ}=\overrightarrow{OQ}-\overrightarrow{OM}=\dfrac13\mathbf a+\dfrac23\mathbf b-\dfrac12(\mathbf a+\mathbf b)=\dfrac16(\mathbf b-\mathbf a)$. Hence $\overrightarrow{PM}=\overrightarrow{MQ}$, and $M$ is the midpoint of $PQ$.

questions.question: The coefficients of $x^2$ and $x^5$ are equal in the expansion of $(x+a)^8$. Find the value of the positive constant $a$.
questions.answer: The coefficient of $x^2$ is ${}^8C_6a^6=28a^6$ and of $x^5$ is ${}^8C_3a^3=56a^3$. $28a^6=56a^3$ gives $a^3(a^3-2)=0$, and since $a>0$, $a=\sqrt[3]2$.

questions.question: Find $\dfrac d{dx}\left(x\tan^{-1}(3x)\right)$.
questions.answer: $\dfrac d{dx}\left(x\tan^{-1}3x\right)=\tan^{-1}(3x)+\dfrac{3x}{1+9x^2}$.

questions.question: Hence find $\displaystyle\int\tan^{-1}(3x)\,dx$.
questions.answer: From part (i), $\tan^{-1}(3x)=\dfrac d{dx}\left(x\tan^{-1}3x\right)-\dfrac{3x}{1+9x^2}$. $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{3x}{1+9x^2}dx=\dfrac16\ln(1+9x^2)$ (since $\dfrac d{dx}(1+9x^2)=18x$). So $\displaystyle\int\tan^{-1}(3x)dx=x\tan^{-1}(3x)-\dfrac16\ln(1+9x^2)+C$.

questions.question: The population, $P$, of porgs on the remote island of Ahch-To satisfies $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=\dfrac12P\left(1-\dfrac P{2000}\right)$, where $t$ is the time in years. Initially there are 300 porgs. Find an expression for $P$ in terms of $t$. You may assume that $\dfrac{2000}{P(2000-P)}=\dfrac1P+\dfrac1{2000-P}$.
questions.answer: $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=\dfrac{P(2000-P)}{4000}$, so $\displaystyle\int\left(\dfrac1P+\dfrac1{2000-P}\right)dP=\int\dfrac12dt$. $\ln|P|-\ln|2000-P|=\dfrac t2+C$, so $\dfrac P{2000-P}=Ae^{t/2}$ and $P=\dfrac{2000Ae^{t/2}}{1+Ae^{t/2}}=\dfrac{2000}{1+Be^{-t/2}}$, where $B=\dfrac1A$. $P(0)=300$: $1+B=\dfrac{20}3$, so $B=\dfrac{17}3$. $P=\dfrac{2000}{1+\frac{17}3e^{-t/2}}=\dfrac{6000}{3+17e^{-t/2}}$.

questions.question: The population, $P$, of porgs on the remote island of Ahch-To satisfies $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=\dfrac12P\left(1-\dfrac P{2000}\right)$, where $t$ is the time in years. Initially there are 300 porgs. Find the greatest value of $\dfrac{dP}{dt}$. You do not need to justify that it is a maximum.
questions.answer: $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=\dfrac P2-\dfrac{P^2}{4000}$ is a downward parabola in $P$ with vertex at $P=\dfrac{1/2}{2/4000}=1000$. The maximum value is $\dfrac12(1000)\left(1-\dfrac12\right)=250$ (people per year).

questions.question: Sketch the curves $y=\cos x$ and $y=\sin x$ for $0\le x\le\pi$. Shade the region bounded by $y=\cos x$, $y=\sin x$, and the $y$-axis.
questions.answer: The curves intersect where $\sin x=\cos x$, i.e. $x=\dfrac\pi4$, at the point $\left(\dfrac\pi4,\dfrac{\sqrt2}2\right)$. $y=\cos x$ starts at $(0,1)$ and $y=\sin x$ starts at $(0,0)$. The region lies between them for $0\le x\le\dfrac\pi4$ (cosine above sine). Sketch:

questions.question: The region bounded by $y=\cos x$, $y=\sin x$ and the $y$-axis is rotated about the $x$-axis. Find the volume of the resulting solid.
questions.answer: $V=\pi\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/4}\left(\cos^2x-\sin^2x\right)dx=\pi\int_0^{\pi/4}\cos2x\,dx=\pi\Big[\dfrac12\sin2x\Big]_0^{\pi/4}=\dfrac\pi2$ cubic units.

questions.question: In how many arrangements of the letters of the word TATOOINE are the Ts separated by one or more letters?
questions.answer: Total arrangements: $\dfrac{8!}{2!2!}=10080$. Arrangements with the Ts adjacent (treat TT as one object): $\dfrac{7!}{2!}=2520$. Ts separated: $10080-2520=7560$.

questions.question: The graph $y=P(x)$ of the quartic polynomial $P(x)=x^4-10x^3+bx^2+cx+16$ touches, but does not cross, the $x$-axis at two distinct points. Explain why $P(x)=(x-m)^2(x-n)^2$ for some real numbers $m$ and $n$.
questions.answer: The graph touches without crossing at an $x$-intercept, so each of the two intercepts is a zero of even multiplicity. A quartic has four zeroes counting multiplicity, so each of the two zeroes has multiplicity 2 and the leading coefficient is 1: $P(x)=(x-m)^2(x-n)^2$.

questions.question: The graph $y=P(x)$ of the quartic polynomial $P(x)=x^4-10x^3+bx^2+cx+16$ touches, but does not cross, the $x$-axis at two distinct points. Given that $mn<0$, find the possible values of $m$ and $n$.
questions.answer: $(x-m)^2(x-n)^2=x^4-2(m+n)x^3+\left(m^2+4mn+n^2\right)x^2-2mn(m+n)x+m^2n^2$. Comparing coefficients: $2(m+n)=10$ so $m+n=5$, and $m^2n^2=16$ so $mn=\pm4$. As $mn<0$, $mn=-4$. So $m,n$ are the roots of $t^2-5t-4=0$: $t=\dfrac{5\pm\sqrt{41}}2$. Hence $\{m,n\}=\left\{\dfrac{5+\sqrt{41}}2,\dfrac{5-\sqrt{41}}2\right\}$ (either way round).

questions.question: Use the substitution $y=u(x)\cos x$, where $u$ is some function of $x$, to solve the differential equation $y'\cos x=y\sin x+\cos x\sin x$.
questions.answer: $y'=u'\cos x-u\sin x$. Substituting: $(u'\cos x-u\sin x)\cos x=u\cos x\sin x+\cos x\sin x$. Dividing by $\cos x$: $u'\cos x-u\sin x=u\sin x+\sin x$, so $u'\cos x=(2u+1)\sin x$ and $u'=(2u+1)\tan x$. Separate variables: $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{du}{2u+1}=\int\tan x\,dx$, so $\dfrac12\ln|2u+1|=-\ln|\cos x|+C$. Then $2u+1=A\sec^2x$ and $u=\dfrac{A\sec^2x-1}2$. Hence $y=u\cos x=\dfrac{A\sec x-\cos x}2$.

questions.question:
Shugo Maki hits a ball from a point 1 m above horizontal ground. The origin $O$ is the point on the ground directly below the point of projection. The ball passes directly over a fielder standing 85 m from the origin. A wall of height 5 m is 117.7 m from the origin. The ball is projected with speed $V$ m/s at an angle of elevation $\theta$. Take $g=10$ m/s$^2$. The motion of the ball is modelled by $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=\begin{pmatrix}V\cos\theta\,t\\1+V\sin\theta\,t-5t^2\end{pmatrix}$. (Do NOT prove this.)

On one occasion, Maki hits the ball with speed 34.3 m/s at an angle of elevation of $45^\circ$. At the instant the ball is hit, the fielder runs directly towards the wall at a constant speed of $W$ m/s. Assume that the fielder can catch the ball provided its height does not exceed 2 m. Find the minimum value of $W$ required for the fielder to catch the ball before the ball reaches the wall. Give your answer correct to two decimal places.
questions.answer:
Height $y=2$: $1+V\sin\theta\,t-5t^2=2$, so $5t^2-V\sin\theta\,t+1=0$. With $V\sin45^\circ=V\cos45^\circ=\dfrac{34.3}{\sqrt2}\approx24.254$, the later root (when the ball is descending through 2 m) is $t=\dfrac{24.254+\sqrt{24.254^2-20}}{10}\approx4.809$ s. At this time the ball is at $x=24.254\times4.809\approx116.64$ m, which is before the wall.

The fielder starts at 85 m, so he is at $85+Wt$. For the catch, $85+Wt=V\cos\theta\,t$, so $W=24.254-\dfrac{85}t$. This increases with $t$, so the minimum $W$ corresponds to the earliest time the ball is catchable, $t\approx4.809$: $W\approx24.254-\dfrac{85}{4.809}\approx6.58$ m/s.

questions.question: Shugo Maki hits a ball from a point 1 m above horizontal ground. The origin $O$ is the point on the ground directly below the point of projection. The ball passes directly over a fielder standing 85 m from the origin. A wall of height 5 m is 117.7 m from the origin. The ball is projected with speed $V$ m/s at an angle of elevation $\theta$. Take $g=10$ m/s$^2$. The motion of the ball is modelled by $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=\begin{pmatrix}V\cos\theta\,t\\1+V\sin\theta\,t-5t^2\end{pmatrix}$. (Do NOT prove this.) For a projected speed $V$ and angle of elevation $\theta$, show that the height of the ball when it reaches the wall is $y=1+117.7\tan\theta-\dfrac{5(117.7)^2}{V^2}\sec^2\theta$.
questions.answer: At the wall, $V\cos\theta\,t=117.7$, so $t=\dfrac{117.7}{V\cos\theta}$. Then $y=1+V\sin\theta\cdot\dfrac{117.7}{V\cos\theta}-5\cdot\dfrac{117.7^2}{V^2\cos^2\theta}=1+117.7\tan\theta-\dfrac{5(117.7)^2}{V^2}\sec^2\theta$.

questions.question: Shugo Maki hits a ball from a point 1 m above horizontal ground. The origin $O$ is the point on the ground directly below the point of projection. The ball passes directly over a fielder standing 85 m from the origin. A wall of height 5 m is 117.7 m from the origin. The ball is projected with speed $V$ m/s at an angle of elevation $\theta$. Take $g=10$ m/s$^2$. The motion of the ball is modelled by $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=\begin{pmatrix}V\cos\theta\,t\\1+V\sin\theta\,t-5t^2\end{pmatrix}$. (Do NOT prove this.) Hence, for a projected speed $V$, determine the angle of projection which maximises the height of the ball when it reaches the wall. You do not need to justify that it is a maximum.
